  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">How can a corruption scheme operate for years?

In 2012, Auckland Transport awarded an infrastructure maintenance and services company an eight-year contract to maintain and upgrade public roading in the Auckland region. 

Employees of the company went on to work with suppliers and subcontractors to create false invoices, conceal conflicts of interest and receive personal benefits in exchange for ongoing work. The offending resulted in approximately $1.5 million in losses and multiple criminal convictions.

This new Serious Fraud Office case study published by the Counter Fraud Centre sets out how many of the warning signs were not hidden: 
•  close personal relationships with suppliers
•  repeated awards to the same contractors
•  employees living beyond their apparent means
•  limited segregation of duties and approval controls.

To avoid fraud continuing unchecked for long periods, prevention is about creating an environment where unusual patterns are noticed, questions are encouraged and concerns can be raised safely.

For anyone involved in procurement, contract management, finance, assurance, risk or leadership, this case is a valuable reminder that trust should always be supported by transparency and oversight. The full case study also offers practical examples of red flags, fraudster behaviours and controls that organisations can use to strengthen their counter fraud capability.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Does a New Zealand entity appear to have won contracts over local competitors without clear justification? That’s a red flag.

Fair and transparent procurement processes help ensure contracts are awarded on merit. When information suggests a company is repeatedly winning contracts despite a lack of clear justification, it's important to look closer.

Why this matters:
• It may indicate favouritism, conflicts of interest, or improper influence in the procurement process
• It can undermine confidence in fair competition and value for money
• Unfair contract awards can expose organisations to fraud, corruption, and reputational risks
 
Red flag indicators:
• Repeated contract awards to the same entity without a clear rationale
• Limited evidence of a competitive procurement process
• Local suppliers appearing equally or better qualified but consistently overlooked
• A lack of transparency around evaluation criteria or decision-making
 
What to do:
• Ensure contract awards are based on transparent and objective criteria
• Conduct due diligence on relationships between suppliers and decision-makers
• Escalate concerns to procurement, audit, compliance, or counter-fraud teams
• Report suspicions about unusually successful companies to the Serious Fraud Office
 
Healthy competition and transparency are a cornerstone of good procurement. When contract awards don’t appear to align with capability, value, or process, it’s essential to ask questions and seek assurance that decisions have been made fairly.
 
The SFO is focused on tackling foreign bribery, and procurement decisions that appear to favour particular entities without clear justification are likely to attract heightened scrutiny.</p>
